id: qml-01
title: Quantum feature spaces
paper: Havlicek et al., Supervised learning with quantum enhanced feature spaces (arXiv Apr 2018; Nature 567, 209, 2019)
link: https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.11326
type: Mechanism
cutoff: 2018-04-30
domain: qml
profile: advantage

## expected_verdict
Supported (scoped) for the demonstration; Speculative for advantage. A 2-qubit hardware classifier on data built to fit its own feature map reached ~100% test accuracy. Classical hardness of the kernel is a conjecture, and no advantage is shown.

## I0
Can a quantum feature-map kernel improve classification on a specified distribution?

## evidence
- Feature map UΦ(x) = UΦ(x) H⊗n UΦ(x) H⊗n with diagonal Z / ZZ phases; φi(x) = xi, φ{1,2}(x) = (π−x1)(π−x2) (Fig. 1b, "The data").
- Hardware: IBM 5-transmon device, only 2 qubits used (Q0, Q1); first-order zero-noise extrapolation (1.5× time stretch) on every circuit (Fig. 2a).
- Data: n = d = 2, labels from ⟨Φ(x)|V† Z1Z2 V|Φ(x)⟩ with a random V ∈ SU(4), gap Δ = 0.3; 20 points per label for training and for each test set.
- Variational classifier: depths l = 0–4, SPSA, 250 iterations, 2,000 training shots (R = 200 in the cost), 10,000 shots at test; 3 data sets × 20 test sets per depth; near 100% success for l > 1 (Fig. 3c).
- Kernel estimator: 50,000 shots per kernel entry; Sets I and II 100%, Set III 94.75% over 10 test sets (Fig. 3c, Fig. 4).
- No classical baseline run. Authors: data "chosen so that it can be classified with 100% success to verify the method".
- Hardness: exact single-layer overlap is #P-hard, but additive-error estimation of one layer is classically efficient; hardness of the two-layer map is a conjecture (main text + supplement).

## intake
- Scope: a quantum kernel or variational classifier built on UΦ classifies synthetic 2D data whose labels are generated by the same feature map, on NISQ hardware.
- Regime: 2 qubits, shallow circuits, error-mitigated, 40 training points.
- Assumptions: data is labelled by a function native to UΦ; the UΦ kernel is classically hard to estimate at scale (conjecture); shot noise does not break the kernel's positive semi-definiteness.
- Falsifiers: (a) a classical kernel (RBF, or the exact UΦ kernel simulated classically) matches accuracy on the same data; (b) kernel values concentrate as qubits grow, so a polynomial shot budget cannot resolve them.

## screen
- Must flag: 2 qubits are trivially simulable, so the experiment cannot test advantage; the labels are engineered from the model's own feature map; hardness is conjectured, not proven.
- Must request: a classical baseline on the same data; kernel scaling with qubit count; the supplement's hardness argument.

## retrieval
- Pre-cutoff must-finds: Schuld & Killoran / Schuld et al. on quantum feature-space kernels (cited as independent concurrent work); Rebentrost et al. quantum SVM (needs coherent data access); Mitarai et al. and Farhi & Neven variational classifiers.
- Current-mode critiques: Thanasilp et al. 2022 (exponential concentration from expressivity, global measurement, entanglement, noise); Shaydulin & Wild 2021 (a bandwidth hyperparameter restores performance and makes quantum kernels competitive with classical ones as qubits grow).

## designer
- Compare the UΦ kernel with RBF / polynomial SVMs and with the exact classically simulated UΦ kernel, on the same splits.
- Vary qubits (2 → ≥ 20 in simulation) and track kernel-value variance and the shots needed per entry.
- Add a bandwidth hyperparameter. Success: the quantum kernel beats tuned classical kernels on data not generated by UΦ.

## champion
- An RBF SVM with tuned bandwidth on the same 40 training points, plus the exact UΦ kernel computed classically (cheap at 2 qubits). Both should reach about 100% on this data.

## panel
- Material flaws: no baseline; engineered labels; the n = 2 hardware result is uninformative about scaling.
- Repair: report the classical kernel results and a qubit-scaling simulation; do not block the hardware demonstration itself.

## run
- Recompute in simulation: the ideal kernel matrix for Set III and SVM accuracy on the published construction (Δ = 0.3, 20 per label).
- The hardware run is not reproducible locally: mark BLOCKED for the hardware numbers; simulate only.

## verdict
- Label: Supported (scoped) for "a quantum-kernel classifier runs on NISQ hardware and classifies map-native data"; Speculative for any learning advantage.
- Must say: advantage requires a classically hard kernel, and that is conjectural; later work shows concentration in generic deep or global regimes, mitigated by bandwidth.
- Must not say: the paper shows quantum advantage; or quantum kernels are useless (concentration is conditional).

## audit
- Check: 2 of 5 qubits used; Δ = 0.3; 20 points per label; 50,000 shots per kernel entry; Set III = 94.75%; hardness stated as a conjecture.
- Flag: no classical baseline exists in the paper to audit against.

## variants
- Bandwidth-scaled UΦ kernels at 10–30 qubits on non-engineered data, compared with tuned RBF. Cheapest follow-up: a classical simulation of the concentration curve.
